\chapter{Ram-Ram Sa: A Greeting the Hand Can Make}
\label{ch:mw-ram-ram-sa}
\hlchaptermodality{1}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can recognise, read, say, copy, and write the respectful Marwadi greeting \mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}, and answer it with the same greeting.}

A two-line authentic greeting exchange followed by independent written recall, using only signs and language taught in the chapter.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ra]{\mw{र} — one sign, and the beginning of a greeting}

\label{lesson:MW-W01-ra}



\begin{quote}
You do not need an alphabet first. Today your eye and hand need one sign.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — notice the sign}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{र}} — \emph{ra}
\end{quote}

Devanagari consonants carry a short \emph{a} by default, so this is \textbf{ra}, not a bare \emph{r}. The \emph{r} is a quick tongue-tip tap.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Put a finger over \textbf{\mw{र}} and follow the printed shape. Then copy it three times, large and slow. Say \emph{ra} each time your pen stops.

This lesson asks you to copy the shape you can see. It does not invent one universal stroke order where school traditions differ.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Cover the model. Point to the one you copied most clearly and say its sound.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ā]{\mw{ा} — make \emph{ra} into \emph{rā}}

\label{lesson:MW-W01-aa-matra}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\mw{र}}. (\emph{ra}.) Copy it once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — add one mark}
The mark \textbf{\mw{ा}} sits on the right of a consonant and lengthens its vowel:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{र}} \emph{ra} + \textbf{\mw{ा}} \emph{ā} = \textbf{\mw{रा}} \emph{rā}
\end{quote}

Hold \emph{ā} steady; do not turn it into English \emph{ray}.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item copy \textbf{\mw{र}}
  \item add \textbf{\mw{ा}} on its right
  \item read the result: \textbf{\mw{रा}} \emph{rā}
\end{itemize}

Do that three times. On the last copy, wait five seconds after looking at the model before you write.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which is \emph{ra}: \textbf{\mw{र}} or \textbf{\mw{रा}}? Which is \emph{rā}?
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rām]{\mw{राम} — your first whole written word}

\label{lesson:MW-W01-raam}



\begin{quote}
Write \textbf{\mw{रा}} after looking away from the model. Check it, then begin.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — add \mw{म}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{म}} — \emph{ma}
\end{quote}

Join it to the piece you know:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{रा}} \emph{rā} + \textbf{\mw{म}} \emph{ma} = \textbf{\mw{राम}} \emph{rām}
\end{quote}

At the end of this word, the built-in vowel of \textbf{\mw{म}} is not pronounced in ordinary speech. Read the whole word \emph{rām}.

\subsection*{Writing — from copy to memory}
1. copy \textbf{\mw{म}} twice 2. copy \textbf{\mw{राम}} once while looking 3. hide the model for ten seconds 4. write \textbf{\mw{राम}} from memory, then compare

If the memory copy stalls, return only to the missing sign.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\mw{राम}} without using the romanization. Then write it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sa]{\mw{स} — a second consonant}

\label{lesson:MW-W01-sa}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\mw{राम}}, then write it from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — notice and copy}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{स}} — \emph{sa}
\end{quote}

Like \textbf{\mw{र}}, this consonant carries a short \emph{a}. Do not confuse the two:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{र}} \emph{ra} · \textbf{\mw{स}} \emph{sa}
\end{quote}

Finger-trace \textbf{\mw{स}}, then copy it three times. Say \emph{sa} as each copy finishes.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Cover the large model and write \textbf{\mw{स}} once from the copy you remember.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sā]{\mw{सा} — reuse a mark instead of learning a new rule}

\label{lesson:MW-W01-saa}



\begin{quote}
What did \textbf{\mw{ा}} do to \textbf{\mw{र}}? Apply the same change to \textbf{\mw{स}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — assemble}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{स}} \emph{sa} + \textbf{\mw{ा}} \emph{ā} = \textbf{\mw{सा}} \emph{sā}
\end{quote}

The writing rule is old; only the combination is new. In the greeting you are building, \textbf{\mw{सा}} is a respectful form of address.

\subsection*{Writing — delayed copy}
Copy \textbf{\mw{सा}} once. Look away for ten seconds, say \emph{sā}, and write it again. Then copy the two pieces with a space:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{राम} \mw{सा}}
\end{quote}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\mw{राम} \mw{सा}}. Circle the two copies of \textbf{\mw{ा}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rām-rām sā]{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा} — your first complete Marwadi greeting}

\label{lesson:MW-C01-raam-raam-saa}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\mw{राम}} and \textbf{\mw{सा}} separately. You already own every sign in today's line.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — meet the greeting}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा।}} — \emph{Rām-rām sā.} — a respectful greeting
\end{quote}

Repeat \textbf{\mw{राम}}, then add respectful \textbf{\mw{सा}}. Rajasthan Sahitya Akademi's \emph{Jāgtī Jot} prints this exchange:

\begin{quote}
A: \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा।}}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
B: \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}, \mw{राम}-\mw{राम।}}
\end{quote}

That attestation is why this track begins here rather than substituting a Hindi greeting merely because the scripts are shared.

\subsection*{Your turn — use and write it}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Hear:} \emph{rām-rām sā}{]} {[}YOU ANSWER: \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}}{]} {[}YOU SAY: the line without romanization
  \item \emph{Copy:} \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}} once, keeping the hyphen and space
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Hide the line. Say the greeting once; then write as much as you can remember.

Source: \href{https://rsad.artandculture.rajasthan.gov.in/content/dam/doitassets/art-and-culture/Rajasthani-Bhasha-Sahitya-Avm-Sanskriti-Academy-Bikaner/pdf/jjpdf/JJ\_All\_Pdf/August-September\%202018\%20E-Ank.pdf}{Rajasthan Sahitya Akademi, \emph{Jāgtī Jot}, August–September 2018}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — hear it, answer it, write it}

\label{lesson:MW-C01-practice}



\begin{quote}
With the page covered, write \textbf{\mw{राम}} and \textbf{\mw{सा}} separately. Check only after both are down.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
A: \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा।}}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
B: \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}, \mw{राम}-\mw{राम।}}
\end{quote}

Run both voices once. Then cover B and answer A aloud. Switch roles.

\subsection*{Your turn — four-skill checkpoint}
1. \textbf{Listen:} ask someone or a screen reader to say \emph{rām-rām sā} without showing the text; identify it as a greeting. 2. \textbf{Speak:} give the greeting without reading. 3. \textbf{Read:} read \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}} without romanization. 4. \textbf{Write:} close the book for fifteen seconds, then write \textbf{\mw{राम}-\mw{राम} \mw{सा}} from memory. Check the repeated word, hyphen, space, and final \textbf{\mw{सा}}.

Writing counts only if the model was hidden. Copying was the ramp; this is recall.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
If one sign stalled, mark that sign and repeat only its short lesson tomorrow.
\end{tcolorbox}
